newsitem.title: INDIA: Little but scorn for India's politicians.
newsitem.headline: Little but scorn for India's politicians.

text.p: Petty, manipulative, undignified, petulant, crass, reckless -- Indian newspapers had tough words on Saturday for the political class that toppled the centre-left government after only 10 months in office.

Editorial writers poured most of their scorn on Congress president Sitaram Kesri, who provoked Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's downfall with his surprise decision to revoke support for the minority coalition.
The dailies were kinder towards Deve Gowda -- an outsider to New Delhi who says he never wanted the job -- although even his alliance which fell on Friday came in for a broadsheet thumping.

"The people will never forgive the major political players for having pushed them into the throes of a parliamentary and constitutional crisis within 10 months of the 11th general election last year," the Tribune said in an editorial headlined, "After the Farce".
"Those who have come to occupy the seats of power are small men in big shoes," the Asian Age said. "The current round of politics is not about issues and consequences. It is to settle scores."
The Tribune said: "We have small-time operators and big-sized manipulators."
Kesri, 77 years old and a follower of Mahatma Gandhi, was the main target for abandoning Deve Gowda for no apparent reason beyond personal pique.
"Never in the history of India's Grand Old Party has there been an instance of such crass, unthinking irresponsibility," the Indian Express said.

The Business Standard said: "Mr Kesri has not only provided the undignified spectacle of an old man in a hurry to get nowhere, he has also been seen to be someone driven primarily by the need to bring down the government so as to stop various cases that were closing in on not just him but also senior leaders close to him."

"The proud traditions of India's parliamentary democracy were unfairly compromised yesterday for the flimsiest and most capricious of reasons," the Hindu said in an editorial entitled, "What a Shame!"

"It is a trenchant comment on the golden jubilee of our independence that a government which enjoys 68 percent of the votes polled could be threatened with summary overthrow not for reasons of high principle or moral imperatives, but out of petty jealousies and reckless desires of self-aggrandisement," said the Times of India.
"The current charade has cost us an incalculable loss on many fronts, economic, industrial and diplomatic."

Several dailies lauded Deve Gowda's government for smoothing ties with India's South Asian neighbours including Pakistan and presenting a budget for the fiscal year beginning on April 1 that they said would bolster the economy.

"A government has been toppled in the budget session and one of the busiest foreign policy seasons ever on grounds -- mostly unstated in today's debate -- that would make Alice in Wonderland seem like serious business," the Indian Express said.
"Spare a thought for the poor Indian who will still go out voting at the peak of summer for the second consecutive year," it added.
